title: Serving runtime: architecture, kernel scheduling, profiling playbooks and benchmarking suite (comprehensive)
author: Arielle Park
content:
Summary
-------
This document consolidates the serving runtime architecture, kernel scheduling design, profiling playbooks, benchmarking suite expectations, recent release notes, known issues, and operational runbooks. It is the canonical reference for engineers operating or extending the Redwood serving runtime.

Goals
-----
- Provide a single reference for architecture and operational patterns.
- Describe the kernel scheduling model and common tuning levers.
- Share the profiling and benchmarking playbooks used for performance regressions and capacity planning.
- Capture runbooks for production incidents and actionable troubleshooting steps.

Scope
-----
Applies to: all hosted/dedicated/private serving runtimes and the orchestration layer that selects kernels, batching, KV cache, and routing policies. This document does not cover model training or offline compiler internals.

1) Architecture overview
------------------------
Short intro: Redwood's serving runtime is a multi-layer system optimized for low latency and high throughput on GPU fleets. Key components:

- Request ingress and routing (api-gateway, router)
- Scheduler and kernel selection service (scheduler)
- Execution runtime (worker processes on GPU nodes)
- KV / prefix cache (sharded in-RAM cache + persistent cache for warmups)
- Observability and tracing (metrics, spans, and logs)

High-level flow:
1) Client request arrives at api-gateway.
2) Router applies policy (latency vs cost vs affinity) and forwards to the scheduler.
3) Scheduler decides allocation, batching windows, and kernel variant.
4) Worker executes with chosen kernel, using KV cache if available.
5) Response streamed back; traces and cost telemetry emitted.

2) Kernel selection & scheduling model
-------------------------------------
Design principles:
- Minimize p99 latency while preserving throughput economics.
- Prefer hardware-optimized kernels for hot model shapes.
- Use graceful fallback kernels when optimized kernels are unavailable.

Key concepts:
- Kernel Variant: precompiled kernel tuned for a model shape (sequence length, batch size, precision).
- Scheduling Slot: a short window (default 4ms) where the scheduler accumulates requests to form micro-batches.
- Affinity Tags: constraints that pin workloads to dedicated pools (e.g., reserved customers).

Scheduling heuristics (default):
- For tail-sensitive routes (SLO==latency), scheduler uses small slot (1-2ms) and prefers single-request dispatch.
- For cost-sensitive routes, scheduler aggregates up to max_batch_size or max_slot_timeout (default 16ms).
- Kernel preference order: optimized kernel -> quantized kernel -> generic kernel. Fallbacks are attempted in that order.

Config table (defaults)
| parameter | default | description |
|---|---:|---|
| max_batch_size | 64 | maximum micro-batch size per kernel invocation |
| scheduling_slot_ms | 4 | default slot time window for batching |
| max_slot_timeout_ms | 16 | absolute max wait time before dispatch |
| tail_preference_threshold_ms | 10 | if p95 > threshold, use latency-first policy |

3) Profiling playbook (for performance regressions)
--------------------------------------------------
Tools used:
- perf and nvprof/NSight (GPU-level counters)
- runtime-profiling agent (internal tool that captures traces, kernel times, nvtx markers)
- flamegraph-generator (CPU/GPU CPU-side stacks)
- loadgen (synthetic traffic generator)

Step-by-step procedure:
1) Reproduce at scale: use loadgen with recorded production request distribution (promoted artifact: testvectors/prod_mix_v2).
2) Capture end-to-end traces (trace-level flag: ENABLE_RUNTIME_TRACING=1).
3) Narrow to candidate workloads: identify model, sequence length percentile, and route.
4) Collect kernel-level metrics (latency per kernel, SM utilization, memory bandwidth) with nvprof.
5) Compare against baseline benchmark artifacts stored in s3://redwood-rt-benchmarks/baselines/<model>-<date>.
6) If regression is kernel-localized, run A/B with kernel variants to confirm.

Quick-check checklist:
- Is p99 increased or is it p50?
- Any increase in CUDA memcopy or kernel launch time?
- Are we spilling to host memory? (check device free memory and OOM logs)
- Has input distribution changed (longer sequences or different tokenization)?

Commands (examples):
- run loadgen: ./scripts/loadgen --config configs/prod_mix_v2.yaml --qps 800
- enable tracing on a node: sudo systemctl set-environment ENABLE_RUNTIME_TRACING=1 && systemctl restart runtime-worker
- nvprof snapshot: nvprof --metrics gld_efficiency,sm_efficiency --profile-from-start off --output-profile kernel-profile.nvvp --pid <worker-pid>

4) Benchmarking suite (ownership & expectations)
------------------------------------------------
Purpose: standardized, reproducible benchmarks for kernel selection, batch sizing, quantization profiles, and autoscaling curves.

Components:
- harness/ : test harness for per-model and per-kernel benchmarks (python 3.10, pytest)
- workloads/ : recorded request mixes (prod, interactive, embeddings-heavy)
- results/ : JSON outputs with metrics (latency percentiles, tokens/s, GPU_util)
- baselines/ : canonical baselines per model and hardware generation

Key metrics produced:
- p50, p90, p95, p99 latency (ms)
- tokens_per_gpu_second
- GPU SM utilization (%)
- Memory headroom (MiB)
- Cost-per-1k-tokens (estimated)

Running the suite (example):
1) Checkout repo: git checkout serving-bench && pip install -r requirements.txt
2) Run for model: python -m harness.run --model gpt-large --hw a100-80gb --workload prod --out results/gpt-large-a100.json
3) Upload results to bench dashboard: ./scripts/upload_results results/gpt-large-a100.json

Benchmark configuration table (example)
| field | example | notes |
|---|---|---|
| model | gpt-large | model identifier in model-catalog |
| hw | a100-80gb | hardware tag |
| quant_profile | q4_0 | quantization profile |
| batch_shape | [1,8,16,32] | batch sizes tested |
| seq_lengths | [32,128,1024] | sequence lengths tested |

5) Release notes (summary of recent runtime releases)
-------------------------------------------------------
v2026.11.0 (2026-11-30) - major
- Kernel selector: added dynamic shape profiler for improved kernel matching for variable-length sequences.
- Scheduler: introduced tail_preference_threshold configuration and per-route scheduling policies.
- Profiling agent: added lightweight sampling to reduce observer overhead.
- Fixed: memory leak in KV cache warmup path (regression tracked in GH #4128).

v2026.12.10 (2026-12-07) - patch
- Emergency fix: reduce default scheduling_slot_ms from 8->4 for hosted tier after p99 increases reported on embeddings routes.
- Updated benchmarking harness to record GPU memband metrics.

6) Known issues
---------------
- Issue: p99 spikes on mixed-precision quantized kernels when sequence variance is >5x. Workaround: pin kernel variant to full-precision for affected routes (route config: kernel_override).
- Issue: rare KV cache invalidation causing cold-start latency (incident: INC-2026-09-12). Mitigation: increase cache TTL and enable pre-warm for scheduled rollouts.
- Issue: profiling agent adds ~1-2% CPU overhead when ENABLE_RUNTIME_TRACING=1; use sampled tracing in production.

7) Runtime runbooks (operational playbooks)
-----------------------------------------
A) High p99 latency (customer impact)
1) Pager on-call team; collect top-level metrics: p50/p95/p99, QPS, GPU_util, mem_free.
2) Run quick profiler: ./tools/quick_snapshot --duration 30s --nodes affected
3) If kernel-bound (nvprof indicates high kernel_latency): rollback last kernel variant rollout and scale up dedicated pool.
4) If scheduling/backpressure (high queue length): reduce scheduling_slot_ms for affected route and increase pool capacity.
5) Postmortem: create postmortem in confluence/oncall-and-incident-response and tag reviewers.

B) OOM on GPU worker
1) Pull /var/log/runtime/oom.log and identify model and input shape.
2) If transient, evict low-priority batches and retry.
3) If repeatable, pin the route to a smaller batch_shape or increase node memory class.

Commands to inspect (ops):
- kafka consumer for request trace: kafka-console-consumer --topic runtime-traces --from-beginning --max-messages 1000 \
  --bootstrap-server kafka.prod:9092 --property print.key=true
- check active kernels: curl -s http://<node>:9090/metrics | grep kernel_active

8) Team wiki & further reading
--------------------------------
- See internal pages: Serving runtime reference, Kernel tuning experiments, Bench dashboard (links in related_pages).
- Weekly office hours: runtime-team-office-hours (Wednesdays 11:00 UTC) for ad-hoc troubleshooting.
- Contact owners: scheduler (team: serving-runtime, owner: kiran.patel@redwood.ai), profiling (sofia.martinez@redwood.ai).

Appendix: artifacts and storage locations
---------------------------------------
- Bench results bucket: s3://redwood-rt-benchmarks/ (read-only for most engineers)
- Profiling snapshots: /mnt/profiles/<date>/node-<id>-nvprof.nvvp
- Baselines and test vectors: git@repo:redwood/serving-bench.git (folder: baselines/)
